Professor '''Vivian Yam Wing-wah''' (born 10 February 1963)<ref name=wiley>{{cite journal |title=Vivian Wing-Wah Yam |journal=Angewandte Chemie International Edition |date=10 June 2014 |volume=53 |issue=24 |pages=6034–6035 |doi=10.1002/anie.201400644}}</ref> CSci, CChem, FRSC,<ref name=Yam/> is a Hong Kong [[chemist]]. Yam is the youngest female member ever to be elected to the [[Chinese Academy of Sciences]]. She was a 2011 [[L'Oréal-UNESCO Awards for Women in Science]] laureate<ref name=Ahmed2013 /> "for her work on light-emitting materials and innovative ways of capturing [[solar energy]]."<ref name=UNESCO>{{cite web|title=Natural Sciences| date=November 2011 |url=http://www.unesco.org/archives/multimedia/index.php?s=films_details&pg=33&id=2161|publisher=[[UNESCO]]|access-date=8 March 2014}}</ref>

==Early years and education==
Vivian Wing-Wah Yam was born in [[British Hong Kong]]. Her father was a civil engineer, although Yam says that neither he nor her mother steered her toward her career. Yam cites being intrigued by the sight of mercury and a workaholic and pregnant biology teacher who taught her up to the very last minute.<ref name=Ahmed2013/>

Yam attended an Anglican grammar school. She received her B.Sc. in chemistry (1985) and PhD (1988) degrees<ref name=LIFM>{{cite web|title=Prof. Vivian Wing-Wah Yam visited Lehn {{not a typo|Institute}} and gave Lecture on Jan 8, 2014|url=http://ce.sysu.edu.cn/Item/20036.aspx|publisher=Lehn Institute of Functional Materials|access-date=8 March 2014|archive-date=2 August 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190802043152/http://ce.sysu.edu.cn/Item/20036.aspx|url-status=dead}}</ref> at the [[University of Hong Kong]] (HKU) where she was on the [[badminton]] team, studying under [[Chi-Ming Che]].

==Career==
In 1988, she became a junior faculty member at the Department of Applied Science, [[City University of Hong Kong|City Polytechnic of Hong Kong]]; at the time, there were no facilities at all for teaching chemistry. She helped with establishing the first chemistry books in the library as well as ordering the first beakers and chemicals.<ref name=Ahmed2013/> Yam's work took her to [[Caltech]] in the late 1980s, where she investigated excited state spectrocsopy under [[Harry B. Gray]]. After a spell at the [[University of Rochester]] (with David G. Whitten) in 1990 she went to study at the [[Imperial College London]] in 1991 (with the Nobel laureate [[Geoffrey Wilkinson]]) and stayed until 1992.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Shamakov |first=Sergey |title=Q&A with Professor Vivian Yam |journal=Energy Fuels |date=Nov 22, 2021 |volume=35 |issue=23 |doi= 10.1021/acs.energyfuels.1c03289 |pages=18845–18847}}</ref> Her research turned to organometallic synthesis "studying the luminescence of complexes with metal–metal interactions". She worked with [[tetraethyllead]] which at the time was not a banned additives for petrol. This work was on the border between organic and inorganic chemicals.<ref name=Ahmed2013/>

Yam has been associated particularly with the elements osmium, platinum and ruthenium.<ref name=Ahmed2013/> She joined the HKU faculty in 2001 where she is the Philip Wong Wilson Wong Professor of Chemistry and Energy. Yam became a [[Fulbright Scholar]] in 2007.<ref name=croucher /> 
{{Quote box
 | quote  ="My research team focuses on new classes of photoactive materials based on organometallics with new properties by combining components associating metal atoms and organic molecules that absorb or emit light."<ref name=spie.org>{{cite web|title=Vivian Wing-Wah Yam|url=http://spie.org/x87693.xml|publisher=[[SPIE]]|access-date=8 March 2014}}</ref> 
 | source =
 | width  =25%
 | align  =right
}}
Yam was elected to the Chinese Academy of Sciences in 2001, aged 38, becoming the youngest female member.<ref name=Ahmed2013>{{cite journal|last=Ahmed|first=Farooq|title=Profile of Vivian W.-W. Yam|journal=PNAS|date=May 14, 2013|volume=110|issue=20 |doi= 10.1073/pnas.1307201110 |pages=7964–7966|pmid=23650373|pmc=3657806|bibcode=2013PNAS..110.7964A|doi-access=free}}</ref> The previous holder of this record was, Che, Yam's earlier mentor.<ref name=Ahmed2013/> She was elected a Fellow of the [[TWAS|Academy of Sciences for the Developing World]] in 2006 and a member of the Foreign Associate of [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 2012.<ref name=LIFM />

==Application==
Yam's research deals with [[organic light emitting diodes]] which are brighter and more efficient that the older light emitting diodes; her chemistry has enabled much more efficient displays to be created for mobile phones and laptops. These [[OLED]]s can be deposited on clear plastic, glass or more unusual materials to also create improved car headlamps and larger flat television screens. Yam quotes that nearly a fifth of the world's power is used to create lighting. Creating more efficient lighting will significantly affect the world's power consumption. She believes internal quantum theory indicates that we may develop lamps based on metal containing chemicals that are 100% efficient.<ref name=Ahmed2013/>

==Awards and honours==
Her awards include the HKU Outstanding Researcher Award (1999–2000), Croucher Foundation Senior Research Fellow (2000–01), Ten Outstanding Young Persons of Hong Kong in 2002, Outstanding Women Professionals and Entrepreneurs Awards (2005), [[State Natural Science Award]] (Second Class, 2005), the Royal Society of Chemistry Centenary Lectureship & Medal (2005/06), and the Japanese Photochemistry Association Lectureship Award for Asian and Oceanian Photochemist Eikohsha Award, (2006), HKU Distinguished Research Achievement Award (2006/07), Hong Kong Outstanding Women Professionals and Entrepreneurs Award (2008), [[Ho Leung Ho Lee Prize]] for Scientific and Technological Progress (2011), the L'OREAL-UNESCO for Women in Science Award (2011), the 13th World Outstanding Chinese Award (2013).<ref name=LIFM /><ref name=croucher>{{cite web|title=Professor Vivian YAM Wing Wah|date=19 May 2011 |url=http://www.croucher.org.hk/professor-vivian-yam-wing-wah|publisher=Croucher Foundation|access-date=8 March 2014}}</ref> and the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]]'s [[Ludwig Mond Award]] (2015).<ref name="RSC-2015">{{cite web|url=http://www.rsc.org/ScienceAndTechnology/Awards/LudwigMondAward/2015-Winner.asp|title=RSC Ludwig Mond Award 2015 Winner|date=5 May 2015|publisher=[[Royal Society of Chemistry]]|access-date=26 May 2015}}</ref> Asteroid [[83363 Yamwingwah]], discovered by [[Bill Yeung]] in 2001, was named in her honour.<ref name="MPC-object" /> The official {{MoMP|83363|naming citation}} was published by the [[Minor Planet Center]] on 17 May 2011 ({{small|[[Minor Planet Circulars|M.P.C.]] 75104}}).<ref name="MPC-Circulars-Archive" /> In 2016, she became a laureate of the [[Asian Scientist 100]] by the ''[[Asian Scientist]]''.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.asianscientist.com/as100/ |title=The Asian Scientist 100 |author= <!--Not stated--> |publisher= [[Asian Scientist]] |access-date= 13 March 2025 }}</ref>

==Personal life==
In 1990, she married Patrick Shing-Tat Mak ({{lang-zh|c=麥成達}}) whom she met in Che's laboratory, where they conducted research together.<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://eastweek.my-magazine.me/main/11331 | script-title=zh:沒科研我會病 任詠華 - 名人薈 - 名人專訪}}</ref> They have two daughters.
